questions.prompt: For a feedback system with DC loop gain \(T_0\), the static (DC) fractional gain error relative to the ideal \(1/f\) is
questions.explanation:
\(G_{cl}=\dfrac1f\cdot\dfrac{T_0}{1+T_0}=\dfrac1f\left(1-\dfrac{1}{1+T_0}\right)\). The shortfall is \(\dfrac{1}{1+T_0}\approx\dfrac{1}{T_0}\).
• \(\dfrac{T_0}{1+T_0}\) is the ratio actual/ideal, not the error.
• \(1/f\) is the ideal gain itself.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a 'dynamic' error in a feedback system, as opposed to a static error?
options: An error caused only by tolerances in the feedback element f
An error that grows with signal frequency (or shows up in transients) because the loop gain \(|T(j\omega)|\) falls at high frequency
An error that exists only at DC
An error caused by the system being switched on
questions.explanation:
The static error \(1/(1+T_0)\) uses the DC loop gain. At higher frequencies \(|T(j\omega)|\) drops (above the loop's dominant pole it falls 20 dB/decade), so the error \(\left|\dfrac{1}{1+T(j\omega)}\right|\) rises, in magnitude and phase. A step response that settles with a time constant is the same effect in the time domain.
• Tolerances in the feedback element set the IDEAL gain \(1/f\), they are not a loop-gain error.

questions.prompt: The loop gain is \(T(jf)=\dfrac{1000}{1+jf/100\ \mathrm{Hz}}\). For a 10 kHz sine, what is the magnitude of the error ratio \(\left|\dfrac{s_{err}}{s_{in}}\right|=\left|\dfrac{1}{1+T}\right|\), in percent?
questions.explanation:
\(T(j10^4)=\dfrac{1000}{1+j100}=\dfrac{1000(1-j100)}{10001}=0.09999-j9.999\).
\(1+T=1.09999-j9.999\), \(|1+T|=10.06\), so \(|1/(1+T)|=9.941\%\).
At DC the error was 0.1%; at 10 kHz, where \(|T|\approx10\), it is about 10%. Common mistake: using \(1/(1+|T|)=9.1\%\), which ignores that \(T\) is almost purely imaginary here.

questions.prompt: The same loop (\(T=\dfrac{1000}{1+jf/100\ \mathrm{Hz}}\)) has \(f=0.01\), so the ideal gain is 100. What is the closed-loop gain MAGNITUDE \(\dfrac1f\left|\dfrac{T}{1+T}\right|\) at 10 kHz?
questions.explanation:
\(\left|\dfrac{T}{1+T}\right|=\dfrac{|0.09999-j9.999|}{|1.09999-j9.999|}=\dfrac{9.9995}{10.059}=0.99407\), so \(|G_{cl}|=99.41\).
Only 0.6% low in magnitude, even though the error ratio is about 10%. The error is mostly in QUADRATURE (90° out of phase), so it mainly shifts the phase instead of shrinking the magnitude.

questions.prompt: A feedback system with ideal gain 10 (\(f=0.1\)) and DC loop gain \(T_0=99\) receives a 1 input step. What is the output after it has settled?
questions.explanation:
After settling, the DC loop gain applies: \(y=\dfrac1f\cdot\dfrac{T_0}{1+T_0}\times1=10\times\dfrac{99}{100}=9.9\). A 1% static error remains forever; the transient only decides how fast you get there.
• 10 would need \(T_0=\infty\).
• 9.09 is \(10/(1+0.1)\), a mis-use of the formula.
• 10.1 applies the 1% error with the wrong sign: feedback systems fall SHORT of \(1/f\).

questions.prompt: In the 10 kHz example, the error ratio \(|1/(1+T)|\) was about 10%, but the closed-loop gain magnitude was only 0.6% low. Why the difference?
options: Because the error ratio formula is wrong at high frequencies
Because the ideal gain \(1/f\) changes with frequency
Because 10% and 0.6% are the same error expressed in dB
At 10 kHz \(T\) is almost purely imaginary, so the error adds at nearly \(90^\circ\): it mostly creates a phase error, and the magnitude changes only to second order
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+T}\). With \(T\approx-j10\), the error term is \(\approx\dfrac{1}{1-j10}\approx j0.1\): perpendicular to 1. Adding a perpendicular 0.1 to 1 changes the length by only \(\sqrt{1+0.01}-1\approx0.5\%\) but rotates it by \(\approx5.7^\circ\).
So a single 'percent error' isn't enough at high frequency; magnitude and phase errors behave differently.

questions.prompt: For the same loop at 10 kHz (\(T=\dfrac{1000}{1+j100}\)), what is the phase of the closed-loop gain relative to the ideal, \(\angle\dfrac{T}{1+T}\), in degrees?
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=\dfrac{0.09999-j9.999}{1.09999-j9.999}\). Angles: numerator \(-89.43^\circ\), denominator \(-83.72^\circ\); difference \(=-5.705^\circ\).
About \(-5.7^\circ\) of phase lag (\(\approx-\tan^{-1}(1/|T|)\)), while the magnitude was only 0.6% low.

questions.prompt: A unity-feedback loop has loop gain \(L(s)=\dfrac{8}{s}\), an integrator. The reference is a ramp \(r(t)=0.5t\). What is the steady-state tracking error \(e=r-y\)?
questions.explanation:
\(E(s)=\dfrac{1}{1+L}R(s)=\dfrac{s}{s+8}\cdot\dfrac{0.5}{s^2}\). Final value theorem: \(e_\infty=\lim_{s\to0}sE(s)=0.5/8=0.0625\). An integrator removes the error for a constant reference but leaves a constant lag of \(0.5/K\) when following a ramp.
• 0 holds for a step reference, not a ramp.
• The error grows without bound only if the loop has no integrator.
• 4 multiplies instead of dividing.
questions.figure_alt: Ramp reference r (solid) and the output y (dashed), which follows it with a small constant lag.

questions.prompt: Preview of P, PI and PID control. A plant \(P(s)=\dfrac{2}{s+1}\) is controlled with a proportional gain \(K_p=4\) in a unity-feedback loop. What is the steady-state error for a unit step reference?
questions.explanation:
The DC loop gain is \(K_pP(0)=4\times2=8\), so \(e_\infty=1/(1+8)=0.111\). Proportional control always leaves a static error with a plant like this, which motivates integral action.
• \(1/8\) uses T instead of \(1+T\).
• 0.25 ignores the plant's DC gain of 2.
• 0 needs an integrator in the loop.

questions.prompt: Preview of PID control. Why does adding integral action, \(C(s)=K_p+K_i/s\), remove the steady-state error for a constant reference?
options: It makes the loop faster, and a faster loop has no error
It adds damping, which cancels the error
The \(1/s\) term makes the DC loop gain infinite, so the static error \(1/(1+T_0)\) goes to zero
It reduces the loop gain at DC
questions.explanation:
The static error is \(1/(1+T_0)\), with \(T_0\) the DC loop gain. An integrator has infinite gain at DC, so the error must settle to zero. Put another way, the integrator's output can only stop changing when its input, the error, is zero.
• Speed and error are separate: a fast proportional loop still has a static error.
• Damping affects the transient, not the final value.
• The integrator raises the DC gain; it does not lower it.

questions.prompt: Preview of integrator windup. A loop with integral action drives an actuator that saturates at its maximum during a large setpoint change. What happens to the integrator, and why is that a problem?
options: The integrator automatically stops when the actuator saturates
Saturation raises the loop gain, which removes the error faster
Nothing: saturation only affects proportional control
The error stays large while the actuator is pinned, so the integrator keeps charging; it then needs a long time of opposite error to unwind, causing large overshoot
questions.explanation:
While the actuator is pinned, the loop is effectively open: more controller output does nothing, but the integrator keeps summing the error. Once the output nears setpoint, the over-charged integrator keeps the actuator pinned until the error has been negative long enough to discharge it, which causes overshoot. Anti-windup schemes stop or bleed the integrator during saturation.
• A plain integrator has no idea the actuator saturated.
• Saturation lowers the effective loop gain to zero.
• Integral action is precisely the part affected.
